title: The 48 Laws of Power
author: after Robert Greene
body:
The 48 Laws of Power - A Five-Minute Masterclass

Power is not simply about controlling people. It is about understanding human nature, managing perception, choosing your battles, and knowing when to speak, act, wait, or walk away.

Here are the 48 lessons, distilled.

1. Never make the person above you feel threatened. Show your value without making powerful people feel replaceable.

2. Do not rely blindly on friends. Friendship can cloud judgment. Sometimes former rivals are more motivated to prove their loyalty.

3. Keep your intentions private. You do not need to reveal every plan before it is ready.

4. Say less than necessary. The more you speak, the more opportunities you create to weaken your position.

5. Protect your reputation. Trust and credibility can take years to build and minutes to destroy.

6. Make yourself visible. Excellent work has limited value if nobody knows it exists.

7. Leverage the strengths of others. You do not have to personally perform every task. Build systems and teams that multiply your impact.

8. Create reasons for people to come to you. Position yourself so others seek your expertise, resources, or opportunities.

9. Win through results, not arguments. Demonstration is often more persuasive than debate.

10. Protect your environment. Constant negativity, chaos, and destructive behavior can spread. Choose your circle carefully.

11. Become valuable. Develop knowledge or capabilities that make your contribution difficult to replace.

12. Strategic honesty builds trust. A sincere gesture at the right moment can lower defenses.

13. When asking for help, explain the benefit to the other person. People respond more strongly to mutual value than obligation.

14. Listen like a friend and observe like a strategist. Understanding people requires attention to what they say, what they avoid, and what motivates them.

15. Resolve serious threats completely. Do not allow recurring problems to survive because you were unwilling to address their root cause.

16. Absence can increase value. Constant availability can reduce appreciation. Give people room to recognize your contribution.

17. Avoid becoming completely predictable. If everyone knows exactly what you will do, your options become easier to control.

18. Do not isolate yourself. Information, relationships, and perspective come from staying connected.

19. Know who you are dealing with. Different personalities require different approaches.

20. Maintain independence. Do not become unnecessarily trapped by another person's agenda.

21. Never underestimate what others may reveal when they think you are harmless. You do not always need to prove how clever you are.

22. When you are weaker, sometimes yielding is smarter than fighting. Temporary retreat can create time, information, and opportunity.

23. Concentrate your resources. Focused energy usually beats scattered effort.

24. Master diplomacy. Understand timing, etiquette, influence, and how to navigate different personalities without unnecessary conflict.

25. Reinvent yourself. Do not allow old labels to permanently define what you can become.

26. Protect yourself from unnecessary blame. Create clear responsibilities, processes, and boundaries.

27. People want something to believe in. A strong mission can create extraordinary commitment, but never exploit that trust.

28. Act decisively once the decision is made. Hesitation after commitment often produces worse results than an imperfect decision executed well.

29. Think beyond the first move. Consider consequences, second-order effects, and the likely ending before beginning.

30. Make excellence look controlled. Preparation should create calm execution, not visible chaos.

31. Shape the available choices. Good strategy often means designing options where multiple outcomes still benefit you.

32. Understand people's hopes. People are motivated not only by facts, but by the future they imagine.

33. Discover what motivates each person. Everyone values something: recognition, security, status, autonomy, money, belonging, or purpose.

34. Carry yourself with self-respect. People often take cues from how you present and value yourself.

35. Master timing. The correct move at the wrong moment can still fail.

36. Stop chasing what you cannot control. Attention gives things power. Sometimes indifference is stronger.

37. Presentation matters. Ideas become more memorable when communicated with emotion, imagery, and clarity.

38. Think independently, but understand the environment around you. You do not need to challenge every convention publicly.

39. Pressure reveals information. When circumstances change, people's priorities and intentions often become clearer.

40. Be suspicious of anything that appears completely free. Hidden costs frequently appear later through obligation, dependency, or loss of control.

41. Do not simply imitate a successful predecessor. Learn from them, then create your own identity.

42. Solve problems at their source. When one central cause creates repeated dysfunction, addressing symptoms will never be enough.

43. Influence both logic and emotion. People rarely change because of facts alone. Understand what they care about.

44. Mirroring can create connection and awareness. Reflecting another person's behavior can help you understand them and sometimes expose their own tactics.

45. Introduce change carefully. People may support improvement while resisting sudden disruption. Transformation often works better in stages.

46. Do not present yourself as flawless. Perfection can create distance, resentment, or suspicion. Competence combined with humanity is more relatable.

47. Know when you have won. Success can create overconfidence. Do not destroy a good outcome by pushing unnecessarily further.

48. Stay adaptable. Do not become trapped by one identity, strategy, technology, organization, or way of thinking. Conditions change. Your ability to adapt is one of the greatest forms of power.

And that is the deeper lesson behind all forty-eight laws. Real power is not domination. It is awareness. Awareness of yourself. Awareness of other people. Awareness of timing. Awareness of incentives. And awareness of when not to act.

You do not need to manipulate everyone around you to become powerful. In modern life, many of these principles are better understood as lessons in leadership, negotiation, emotional intelligence, reputation, strategy, and self-control.

Learn the rules so you can recognize the game. Then decide what kind of person you want to be while playing it.

title: Meet Bunlong Heng (Short)
author: Bunlong Heng
body: Hi, my name is Bunlong Heng. I am a Senior Full-Stack Developer with over 12 years of experience building web applications and owning them end to end. I graduated from UMass Lowell with a degree in Computer Science in 2014, and throughout my career I have worked across the entire stack, from React and Node J S to A P I's, databases, cloud, security, and performance. Most recently, I have been working at Thrive. One project I am especially proud of is the Advanced Campaign Editor for the Thrive Business Center. I helped lead and build it using React and Node J S, with backend A P I's and Amazon S three. I also worked heavily on the Reporting Center, including the Keep and Thrive integration, where I helped plan how reporting data should flow between the systems securely and accurately. Performance was a big focus for me there. One of my favorite wins was bringing our dashboard response time down from around five seconds to under half a second. I also worked on observability, security and performance readiness, and mentoring developers. I am A W S certified as both a Solutions Architect Associate and Developer Associate. Lately, though, I have gotten really into auditing. I audit repositories, P R's, Jira epics, and even projects that span multiple repositories. The project I am most excited about is something I built called Repo Audit. Repo Audit reverse-engineers a codebase across ten different engineering lenses, including architecture, security, performance, testing, maintainability, and code quality, and brings everything together into one structured report. I have run more than 500 audits with it so far. But the main reason I built it is actually pretty simple: I want to become a better developer. It lets me go back through my own work, find mistakes, learn from decisions I have made in the past, and bring those lessons into whatever I build next. It also acts as a quality gate. Before I release or open-source something, I can audit it and make sure the code I am putting my name on meets my standards. And as A I gets better, the audits get better too. I can revisit older projects and keep learning from them. That is really how I approach engineering. I love building, I love staying hands-on, and I am always looking for ways to build better software and become a better developer. Thanks for taking the time to learn a little bit about me.

title: Meet Bunlong Heng
author: Bunlong Heng
body: Hi, my name is Bunlong Heng. I am a Senior Full-Stack Developer, and I have been building web applications for over 12 years. I graduated from UMass Lowell with a degree in Computer Science in 2014, and throughout my career, I have always been the kind of developer who likes to own things end to end. I am comfortable moving across the entire stack, from React and Node J S to A P I's, databases, cloud infrastructure, security, and performance. I really enjoy understanding how the whole system works, not just one piece of it. Most recently, I have been working at Thrive. One project I am especially proud of is the Advanced Campaign Editor for the Thrive Business Center. I helped lead and build that application using React and Node J S, with backend A P I's, Amazon S three buckets, and support for themes and plugins. I also spent a lot of time working on the Reporting Center. As part of the Keep and Thrive integration, I helped plan the Reporting Center work for both Phase One and Phase Two. That involved understanding how data should flow between the systems, making sure it was accurate and secure, and helping break a pretty large integration into pieces the team could actually build and deliver. Performance was also a big focus for me. One thing I am really proud of is that we were able to bring our dashboard response time down from around five seconds on average to under half a second. I also worked on observability with Data Dog, created security and performance readiness checklists, and mentored developers around security, code quality, debugging, and production readiness. I am also A W S certified as both a Solutions Architect Associate and Developer Associate. But lately, one thing I have gotten really into is auditing. I audit repositories, P R's, Jira epics, portfolios, Git Hub profiles, and even projects that span multiple repositories. The project I am probably most excited about is something I built called Repo Audit. I wanted a better way to really understand a codebase, not just ask A I to summarize it. So Repo Audit reverse-engineers a repository across ten different engineering lenses, looking at things like architecture, security, performance, testing, maintainability, and code quality, and then brings everything together into one structured report. I have run more than 500 audits with it so far. But for me, the biggest reason I built it is to become a better developer. I can look back at decisions I have made, find mistakes or things I could have done better, learn from them, and carry those lessons into the next thing I build. It also acts as a quality gate for my work. Before I release or open-source something, I can audit it from multiple engineering angles and make sure the code I am putting my name on meets the standards I expect from myself. And as the A I models get better, the audits get better too. I can revisit older projects and discover things I may not have caught before. I think that represents me pretty well as an engineer. I love building, I love staying hands-on, and I am always trying to find ways to become a better developer and build better software. That is really who I am as a Senior Full-Stack Developer. Thanks for taking the time to learn a little bit about me.

title: The North Wind and the Sun
author: Aesop
body: The North Wind and the Sun were disputing which was the stronger, when a traveler came along wrapped in a warm cloak. They agreed that the one who first succeeded in making the traveler take his cloak off should be considered stronger than the other. Then the North Wind blew as hard as he could, but the more he blew the more closely did the traveler fold his cloak around him; and at last the North Wind gave up the attempt. Then the Sun shone out warmly, and immediately the traveler took off his cloak. And so the North Wind was obliged to confess that the Sun was the stronger of the two.
